source.title: Causal Machine Learning: A Survey and Open Problems

accepted.question_text: What standardized benchmark suites and evaluation protocols should be developed for causal supervised learning methods that aim to learn invariant predictors under spurious correlations, so that practitioners can compare methods on common tasks with controlled distribution shifts instead of relying on isolated toy experiments?

evidence.quote: Previous works in invariance learning often evaluate their suggested methods on novel toy experiments instead of a standardized test bed. As a result, practitioners cannot quickly determine the best approach for their problem.

accepted.question_text: How can causal assumptions and intervention-based reasoning be used to connect invariant feature learning with adversarial robustness and meta-learning, for example by treating robust prediction as invariance to perturbations or by learning task-invariant structure that can adapt quickly to unseen tasks?

evidence.quote: We put forward to investigate how causal assumptions may beneﬁt these areas, as it is currently underexplored.

accepted.question_text: Which additional supervision signals beyond class labels should invariant feature learning use, and how should methods combine content-preserving transformations, environment information, high-dimensional environment descriptors, and richer object-or-attribute labels to separate spurious from invariant predictive structure?

evidence.quote: Identifying and exploiting other forms of labels that inform invariant feature learning is an open problem.

accepted.question_text: At what level of abstraction should a causal representation learning system define its latent causal variables, ranging from very low-level variables such as pixels to high-level object variables, so that the resulting structural causal model is both identifiable and useful for efficient, interpretable causal reasoning?

evidence.quote: It is not obvious how practitioners should determine a reasonable level of abstraction for causal representation learning, much less do so automatically [113, 114, 115, 116].

accepted.question_text: Which problem specifications and supervisory signals are sufficient and sensible for causal representation learning, which of them can be relaxed, and what trade-offs arise between stronger supervision, identifiability, realism of data requirements, and automation of learning latent causal structure?

evidence.quote: Can we identify other sensible speciﬁcations or even relax them?
Thus, what kinds of supervisory signals are optimal for CRL, what trade-oﬀs exist, and which signals are reasonable to require, are all open problems.

accepted.question_text: How can structural assignment learning methods for causal generative modeling be scaled from the small causal graphs used in current work to substantially larger causal graphs while still supporting flexible counterfactual generation and accurate modeling of real-world high-order dynamics?

evidence.quote: Hence, how to tackle the scalability of the underlying causal graphs in structural assignment learning remains an open problem.

accepted.question_text: When, why, and by how much does counterfactual data augmentation produced by causal generative models improve downstream generalization relative to non-causal or hand-crafted augmentation methods, and how should such methods be benchmarked using external prediction performance?

evidence.quote: Exploring when and by how much CFDA using causal generative models improves generalization remains an open problem.
Such a benchmarking method is under-explored.

accepted.question_text: How should causal feature-attribution methods and contrastive or counterfactual explanation methods be unified so that a single explanation can communicate both which features must change and which features should remain fixed in order to achieve a desired outcome?

evidence.quote: So far, it is unclear how to unify both classes of methodology best

accepted.question_text: Which approximation strategies can make causal explanation methods computationally tractable and deployable in large-scale systems with many users while preserving enough fidelity, plausibility, and actionability for practical use?

evidence.quote: To make explanations deployable in large-scale systems with many users, approximate methods are highly needed.

accepted.question_text: How can explanation methods remain useful when deployed models, user behavior, or utility functions change over time, so that explanations stay valid under temporal dynamics and distribution shift rather than assuming a static black-box predictor?

evidence.quote: Naturally, these issues arise for model explanations too, and there exists only limited work to address them [165, 166, 167].

accepted.question_text: How can explanation systems be made secure and privacy-preserving against model extraction, decision-boundary reconstruction, membership inference, and attacks that recover causal structure from interactive queries, without making the explanations unusably weak?

evidence.quote: There has been very limited work on guarding explanation methods against such concerns.

accepted.question_text: Given the impossibility result that an attribution method cannot in general be both continuous under small input perturbations and guaranteed to point toward utility-improving recourse directions, what workaround or reformulation can preserve useful forms of robustness and recourse sensitivity in practical explanation systems?

evidence.quote: Future work should therefore consider workarounds to circumvent Fokkema et al. [162]’s impossibility result.

accepted.question_text: How can fairness notions based on equity rather than strict equality be operationalized in machine-learning systems, and in what ways would such equity-based criteria agree with or contradict existing causal fairness definitions?

evidence.quote: An exciting future direction is to operationalize this deﬁnition and examine how it enhances or contradicts existing deﬁnitions of fairness [3].

accepted.question_text: How should causal fairness methods formalize and estimate harm so that they can answer three linked questions: whether an agent’s actions caused harm and by how much, how much harm an action is expected to cause before it is taken, and which actions best balance expected harms against benefits?

evidence.quote: Q1: Did the actions of an agent cause harm, and if so, how much?Q2: How much harm can we expect an action to cause before taking it? Q3: How can we identify actions that balance the expected harms and beneﬁts?

accepted.question_text: What should fairness mean for machine-learning settings beyond prediction, especially for recourse systems, including whether the ability to obtain recourse and the effort required to achieve favorable outcomes are distributed fairly across protected and unprotected groups?

evidence.quote: there is still much work left. For example, the question of whether it is appropriate to perform societal interventions on all individuals in a subgroup.

accepted.question_text: How can causal fairness analyses remain reliable when the required counterfactual or interventional quantities are only partially identifiable, especially under hidden confounding or violated assumptions, and what sensitivity-analysis procedures or realistic simulations are needed to quantify the resulting uncertainty?

evidence.quote: While previous causal fairness work has partly addressed these issues [175, 178, 195], we foresee more important work to be done in sensitivity analysis through realistic simulations

accepted.question_text: Can causal fairness frameworks legitimately model social categories such as race or gender as variables that admit interventions and counterfactual manipulation, or do the moral, political, and sociological features of such categories invalidate standard interventionist assumptions such as modularity?

evidence.quote: Kasirzadeh and Smart [199] review various papers at this intersection between sociology and causal modeling, concluding that social categories often do not admit counterfactual manipulation.

accepted.question_text: When multiple fairness criteria conflict and cannot all be satisfied simultaneously, what principles, objectives, or stakeholder-aware procedures should be used to balance those competing criteria in a causal fairness pipeline?

evidence.quote: Hence, in practice, the trade-oﬀ between multiple admissible criteria has to be balanced.

accepted.question_text: Under what conditions can a model produce unfair predictions even when it is trained on labels that are themselves fair, and how can causal fairness methods detect, stress-test, and prevent this introduced unfairness?

evidence.quote: Minimal work exists investigating when fair training labels may not yield a fair model.

accepted.question_text: What unified evaluation environments and protocols should be adopted for causal reinforcement-learning methods, particularly model-based approaches, so that different algorithms can be compared on overlapping tasks instead of each paper using disjoint environments?

evidence.quote: However, there is no overlap in their evaluation environments.

accepted.question_text: To what extent can the many existing reinforcement-learning formalisms that combine causality, hidden parameters, confounding, or partial observability be rigorously compared and possibly unified, so that practitioners are not forced to navigate a fragmented landscape of near-overlapping models?

evidence.quote: We suggest that future work compares the applicability of diﬀerent formalisms more rigorously and possibly uniﬁes them.

accepted.question_text: How can offline reinforcement learning deconfound observational datasets collected without direct access to the behavior policy or environment, so that learned policies are not driven by confounding biases present in logged data?

evidence.quote: We believe that deconfounding observa- tional data is under-explored in pure oﬄine RL settings, and only a few works have addressed this setup [256].

accepted.question_text: How should reinforcement-learning agents use counterfactual reasoning during decision-making, policy search, credit assignment, or human-in-the-loop interaction, and what carefully designed real-world counterfactual agents would demonstrate benefits beyond observational reasoning alone?

evidence.quote: We hope to see more carefully-designed counterfactual agents for real-world systems that may take inspiration from Bottou et al. [208].
